meeting.title: 2026-09-08 Board of Education’s Teaching, Learning, and Enrollment Committee

segments.text: Okay, this public meeting of the Board of Education's Teaching, Learning, and Enrollment Committee for September 8th, 2026 is called to order. Good afternoon, and welcome to our first meeting of the 26-27 school year for teaching, learning, and enrollment. Tonight's meeting will be mainly focused on hearing from staff about what a well-resourced school looks like. We'll have the opportunity to discuss any upcoming TLG agenda items. Sorry, I'm like still warming up for the school year apparently. And hear from other committee members about what agenda topics they might be interested in. I'll give a little preview of some things that we're going to have on the agendas coming up in the next few months. But first, I will start with myself. My name is Virginia LaForte. I am the board member. I reside in Zone 5, which is northeast Portland, and we'll go ahead and pass it around.
Hi, Rochelle Chase Miller, board member from Zone 4.
Hi, my name is my mic on? Okay, cool. Hi, my name is Eve. I am a senior at Franklin and the student rep on this board or committee.
Well, good evening. My name is Christina Howard and I'm Senior Chief of Economics.
All right. Roseanne, do we have anyone signed up for public comment?
Yes, we do. We have someone virtually. I'll bring her in.
I'm just oh good.
Ellie Buckner.
Hi. I'm trying to get the video going there.
Can you hear me? Hold on, Ellie. We can't hear you. Hold on just a second.
Let me know if there's anything I need to do. There we go. Now we can. Thank you. Excellent. Thank you. Should I start for the two minutes?
Yes, go right ahead.

I'm Ellie Buckner, B-U-C-K-N-E-R. As a parent of two children who attend Buckman Elementary School as our neighborhood school, I am here to continue to advocate for our Title I Buckman neighborhood community during the right-sizing discussions. If the board moves forward with the potential proposal to consolidate Buckman with Abernaff Elementary School. I strongly request that the board considers the consolidated school be housed on the Buckman campus rather than in Latt's edition. Moving Buckman students away from their neighborhood campus introduces severe safety and equity issues for our community. Pedestrian safety and major thoroughfares is a serious concern. Moving Buckman neighborhood families to the Abernathy campus would force young children living north of Burnside to cross two major high-traffic arterial streets, Burnside and Hawthorne. This poses a significant daily safety hazard for walking and biking students. Second, the impact of our Title I could on our Title I community would also be significant. Buckman is a designated Title I school serving a higher percentage of historically underserved and lower-income families. Forcing these families to travel significantly farther to school creates an undue burden, particularly for those who rely on walking in public transit and face scheduling constraints. Housing-compliant student body at Buckman minimizes transportation barriers, and Buckman's campus size is larger than Abernathy's to accommodate the combined student body. I ask the board to please consider student safety and equity for our Title I Buckman neighborhood families in your right-sizing decisions as they come to a conclusion. If the board ultimately decides to consolidate into Abernathy's campus rather than Buckman's, alternatively, please seriously consider adjusting the attendance boundaries for the families who live north of Burnside,
so they're able to attend another elementary school with safer travel paths. Thank you.

Thank you. Appreciate it. I do want to acknowledge, I don't think they may have been there, and I might have just cranked right past them. Directors Engelsman and Split are both joining us virtually. I know that Director Split is on her way in her car, so I will ask her to keep her eyes on the road and say hello. I think, is that it for public comment, Roseanne? Great, thank you. So, thank you for your comments, and let's begin with our overview of what well-resourced schools look like, which is something that we are considering as we are in the process of right-sizing our district. Senior Chief Howard, would you like to introduce this item?

Yes, good afternoon, Board Directors. Today, the team will provide an update on the district's right-sizing work, including a closer look at the working definition of a well-resourced school, and also provide several hypothetical examples that illustrate conditions across PPS. Joining us today are Margaret Calvert, Executive Director of School Planning and Modernization, Dr. Emily Glasgow, Senior Director of PK-12 Core Academics and Dr. Philippe Hreestich, Senior Director of Programs and Pathways. I will now turn it over to Dr. Hristich to kick us off.
Good afternoon. My name is Philip Priestic. I'm proud to serve as the senior director for K-12 Programs and Pathways. Thank you, Board Directors and Student Representative Thompson.

And my name is Emily Glasgow. I'm currently serving as the Senior Director of Pre-K-12 Core Academics. Thank you for the opportunity to present on what we believe is our shared commitment: ensuring that every single child in our city attends a well-resourced school.
Good afternoon. My name is Margaret Calvert. I'm the Executive Director for School Planning and Modernization. We look forward to the conversation this afternoon. Thanks for having us.

As we usually do, we'll begin with our learning targets and success criteria. During our time together, we will explore the impact that stretched resources have had on our schools and how an intentional right-sizing process can mitigate those impacts. Our hope is that by the end of our presentation and discussion, we will all be able to articulate our current challenges and show how right-sizing balances resources to guarantee equitable opportunities for all our students. As I think we all know, we are at a critical juncture in our school district. Our student enrollment has shrunk significantly, but our physical footprint has not. Since the 2018-19 school year, enrollment dropped by more than 6,000 students, yet we operate the exact number of school sites. Compounded by budget reductions, our resources are spread dangerously thin and unevenly across the system. This slide captures some of the intentional work we've done over the years, over the last two decades actually, to adapt to our enrollment and budget realities. As you can see, we adjusted boundaries, transitioned middle schools to K-8s, and back again to middle schools.

We closed programs and consolidated sites. These incremental efforts, unfortunately, haven't solved our structural reality. Spreading limited funds across too many buildings dilutes our ability to provide high-quality programming across all our schools. As a result, we've been forced to split staff across buildings, subsidize low enrollment sites, trim back supports, and collectively feel the growing pinch of resources spread thin. If we do nothing, this pinch will only grow stronger. By 2031-32, our enrollment is projected to decline by another 3,400 students. At that point, only five out of every six elementary schools, six out of seven K-8s, and seven out of eight middle schools will lack the enrollment needed to run complete programs. When enrollment drops, funding drops. Lower enrollment means split-grade classrooms, part-time art,

music teachers, losing electives, high staff turnover, and more impacts on our students, families, and staff. Right-sizing, however, isn't just a conversation about closing buildings. This process is about reestablishing a shared vision of what every child deserves to have in their school and reallocating resources to make that a reality everywhere. What should be true in every neighborhood and at every grade level is a student's experience anchored by four core pillars: stable staffing, rich programming, comprehensive student supports, and safe, well-equipped facilities. In other words, right-sizing should ensure that students at all schools benefit from increasingly stable staffing that allows for grade-level classrooms, teacher collaboration, and less educators split across multiple buildings or roles. It should ensure access to a full range of enrichment and elective offerings, athletics, and intervention supports as needed, access to culturally specific partnerships,
mental health and nursing supports, and family and community resources, and learning within a facility that supports core and enrichment programming.

The good news is that much of this right-sizing work is already underway in our high schools. Thanks to your leadership and other work done with the high school system over the years, our target threshold for comprehensive high schools is now around 1,100 students. Before high school redesign, a small or under-resourced site meant limited AP choices, minimal dual credit offerings, and inconsistent athletic and extracurricular offerings. Today, all of our comprehensive high schools are on track to offer robust college preparatory programming, articulated CTE pathways, dedicated support staff, and universal access to athletics and extracurriculars.

And now you've charged us with working toward the same type of goals in our elementary and middle grades. At last week's board meeting and village table, we heard a need for more detailed information about the vision of well-resourced schools. Today, we're going to offer two stories to try to meet that need: an elementary story and a middle-grade story. Before I start, I want to be clear to note that the composite schools and programs I'm going to describe in these stories are just that. They're composites. While they mirror the conditions of many of our actual schools, they are not specific PPS schools. I want to start with an elementary scenario typical of the current state. Let's imagine that there are three schools, A, B, and C, that are all located within five miles of one another. All serve elementary students. One also serves sixth through eighth graders. One includes a co-located dual language immersion program. Enrollment at these three schools ranges from 200 to 350. Last spring, all three schools experienced the pain of teacher layoffs and staffing reductions. Currently, all three schools are experiencing the pinch of shrinking resources in the following ways.

At least one grade ban, first through second grade or fourth through fifth grade, is blended. Arts educators are split across multiple schools. Libraries are open part, but not all of the week. Middle school students on the K-8 campus are assigned to a limited range of electives. Instructional coach and intervention resources have been reduced or eliminated. Grade-level teacher collaboration is challenging, particularly in the co-located DLI building where enrollment is uneven and curriculum is different across strands. And lunchtime and recess duty staffing is limited, so the single administrator in the building spends two to three hours each day on lunch and recess duty. Now, let's imagine a hypothetical future state for the same three school communities. In this scenario, through a combination of program relocation, grade reconfiguration, and school consolidation, this cluster of schools has been right-sized. Elementary students from schools A, B, and C have been assigned to two K-5 campuses located within three miles of one another.

Middle grade students from the K-8 have been shifted to their neighborhood middle school. Dual language immersion students have been shifted to another nearby DLI site. Enrollment at all of the impacted schools now ranges from 360 to 500, and the following is now true at each impacted site. Students at all grade levels are assigned to single-grade level classrooms. Each site has enough arts allocation to experience the benefits of a full arts program, not just a day or two of arts classes. Libraries at all impacted sites are open more consistently. Instructional coach and intervention resources have been partially or fully restored. All educators, English scholar and DLI, have grade-level peers teaching the same curriculum as them, making collaboration easier and more productive. And more stable full-time staffing in the building allows for a stronger duty schedule, allowing the principals to spend more time on instructional leadership. Now let's move through a similar exercise with middle grades. Today in PPS, we serve 6th through 8th grade students at 28 different school sites. These sites include K-8, 6-8, and K-12 campuses.

Middle grades enrollment at these sites ranges from approximately 75 students to approximately 700 students. Currently, the experience and opportunities of middle-grade students vary considerably in the following ways. In some cases, students take core subjects in blended classrooms. In some cases, students can select from a range of electives, including arts, world language, STEM, etc., where in other cases students are restricted to a small range of pre-assigned electives. Not all middle grades programs are able to offer a full continuum of accelerated math courses. In some programs, instructional coach intervention and climate resources have been reduced or eliminated. Teacher collaboration is challenging, particularly in cases where only one teacher in the building teaches each grade level or content area. And access to learning spaces designed to support physical education, arts, and STEM instruction vary considerably across campuses. On this slide, we can see examples of the ways in which right-sizing could balance out resources across campuses to provide more of the 6th through 8th grade students with a common base of learning opportunities. Through program shifts, grade band reconfigurations, and/or school consolidations,

right-sizing at the middle grades level would balance out resources to ensure that most 6th through 8th grade students have access to the following high school preparatory experiences. Daily grade level standards align instruction in all core content areas, appropriate opportunities for intervention and acceleration as needed, a comprehensive range of elective course offerings, instruction planned and designed by collaborative educator teams, streamlined feeder patterns to support transitions to and from middle school, and a network of community and school-based partnerships, providing a range of in-school and extracurricular support and opportunities. Before we move to questions and discussion, I just want to close with a couple of quick summary comments. First, I want to acknowledge that while we're speaking about this in analytic terms, we're talking about numbers and programs and resources, this is inherently an emotional conversation. Philippe and I, and once upon a time, Margaret, are all PPS parents. We live in the community. We understand that there is a real tension between knowing we need to act and hearing and holding the anxieties and the impacts of our students and our families and our educators. We love our schools, they're the heart of our communities,

and we want to say collectively and out loud that nobody would be having this conversation if we didn't need to be. A parent who attended last week's Village Table summarized this in very simple terms. She said, This, the right sizing, isn't the bad. The bad has already happened. This is the solution to the bad. That stuck with me. I found it to be a helpful framing, so I wanted to offer it here. With that, we want to open up for questions and discussion.
All right, thank you very much. I guess let's go ahead and get started. You want to start? Sure.

Thank you for the presentation and the hypotheticals. Those were very helpful. I'm not sure if I can articulate this question well, so I'm going to try. I don't know if you can say now, but when we think about the future scenarios, are you all looking at any, like, are you looking at any absolutes, like K8s are just not going to be a thing, or split feeders are not going to be a thing, or all DLIs are going to co-locate. Like, is it, are we looking at things that are that concrete kind of by type, or is it more of a situational situation and, like what works best for this neighborhood or block of schools or part of town is what we're going to do versus like an all or nothing.

Appreciate the question, Director Chase Miller. What we are looking at across the system is that there are unique situations in different parts of the city, as you're describing. So, what we are looking for is using all the levers that we have to provide a path for each part of the city. And they vary. So the west side, for example, has fewer elementaries as a whole. There are parts in the southeast that have quite a few elementaries. And so, part of what we're looking at across the system is: what are some general guiding principles that you guys have outlined? Also, looking at some design principles that will be applied differently across different parts of the city. What I would say is that when we look at the regions and thinking about what is present, we also want to be responsive to the pieces that are important to the communities in those schools. And so, while we're moving towards the communities in that part of the city, so as we're moving towards recognizing what's present, and then also, how do we move towards something that provides comparable programming across the city? So it's not, there aren't absolutes like it's all one thing or another, it's going to be a mixture of pieces as we go.

Thank you. That sounds like the best way to be responsive to all of the things that we want to be responsive to. Back last year when we were doing the Jefferson work, there was some conversation about the work that would happen with cloth with right-sizing and kind of pathways to bolster Roosevelt's enrollment. Is that still something that we're taking into consideration as we work through this process? And is there any more you can say about that?

So I think that we I appreciate again the question of and connecting the processes. One of the things that we are looking at is really how do we s build sustainable pathways at each grade level in each part of the city? So we are thinking regionally, is what I would say about how we're approaching the scenario development. And we're recognizing that there are schools at each grade level that we're going to really need to pay attention to enrollment over the next few years. And so we mentioned that we're going to watch closely what the patterns are for both Jefferson and Roosevelt and high school enrollment as coming out of the right-sizing process, or excuse me, the Jefferson sunsetting the Jefferson dual assignment process. That will be hold true not only at high schools, but also at elementaries and at middle schools, that we're trying to be very attentive to where we're seeing that there are schools that are going to be close to or are below the thresholds over time, and we need to address those. Like, what are ways that we can address that? Well, also attending to some of the other considerations that we've talked about, which include things like schools that have recently undergone changes. So it's going to be ideally when we share, you know, bring the scenarios forward that it'll highlight and be explicit about some of those tensions and what the trade-offs are moving forward.

One more question, I'll give other folks a turn. I have heard just kind of floating around in community: why do we have to do closures and consolidations? Why can't we just do boundary changes and balance things out. Can you speak to that?

Yeah, I think it's part of what, it was on one of the slides, if we look back, go back a few. The Southeast Guiding enrollment balancing process looked at all of these things. It looked at boundary changes and grade level reconfigurations and program moves. And part of what we see coming from this is that we simply don't have enough students for the number of sites that we are operating. And so we have seen those changes happen in the last few years and thinking through what that balancing could look like. But there's no sort of magic way of drawing the lines that keeps the right number of students in their right number of schools, and so we're just out of alignment with that. Part of what we talked about here in this slide is that over the last few years we've tried this in a number of different ways that we've looked at boundaries. Some through Sunsetting Jefferson dual assignment was really a boundary decision. Same thing with Southeast Enrollment Balancing, District-wide Boundary Review, that goes back to really 12 years of process, and when we look at the last time that we made the difficult decision to close schools, it was 2012, and that was at Humboldt Elementary. And the last time we've looked at high schools was Marshall in 2011. And so we are,

you know, far from making those decisions at this point, and we've tried a number of processes to try to smooth things out across the city and support really healthy school size, and really the size doesn't dictate the health of the school, but the predictability of staffing and the supports and all the pieces that we talk about do. And so I think that that's what we're experiencing now.

Okay, I had a few questions. Um, so my first question is, how will this or will what will this do to staff? Like, will c a lot of my friends' parents are teachers, so I'm hearing a lot of my mom's scared, my dad's scared, my mom's scared, and so I want to know, like, how this will affect staff? Like, do you have a projected number for how many will get laid off, or how many positions will stay, or that any of that?

I mean, I can start and say, like, that's real. I don't want to acknowledge that staff are nervous and have a lot of anxiety, just like families do in this process. We're facing, as you guys know, a major budget decline over the next several years continuing, regardless of whether we do this process or not, which makes staffing unstable and challenging. Our hope, as if we move through this process and we're able to do some right-sizing, is that over the next five years, we're coming to a place where staffing becomes more stable and consistent. If and when we move programs or consolidate schools, there would be some movement of staff from building to building as part of the process, and that would be driven by contractual agreements and our human resources processes.

But please add. Can I add a couple of more things? Our hope would also be that we have fewer staff who are spread across multiple buildings. We have 54 art positions in our K-5 schools right now in PPS. Of those 54 positions, only four are full-time teachers in a building. Of the 54 are full-time dedicated staff to a building. The rest are split across multiple buildings, which has a tremendous impact on those staff, on those schools, on those students, on those communities, and our teachers are doing an amazing job. So, our hope would be that through this process, it's hard to predict what the staffing funding levels will be and how much staff we will be able to have, but our hope is that it's less about having fewer staff and more about having more staff together, working with our colleagues in dedicated school communities.

Yeah, and then I'll add one thing. I think as we are going through the school year, similar to last year, staffing is driven by enrollment. So, we'll be looking at our enrollment numbers as well as collaborating with many of our labor partners to finalize our staffing. So, while you're hearing about hypotheticals here, no decisions have been been made and we'll be collaborating with others around that.

Okay. Uh thank you. Um my next question is or my last two are actually student-based. So, my first one kind of comes from the public comment earlier. How are will boundaries change as schools are right-sized and will this protect safe travel? Because we were talking about a lot of young kids and like high schoolers, we can figure it out, you know. But like, my elementary school was really close to my house, and I know that my parents couldn't ha did not have time to take me to school every day. And so I'm worried about students in especially lower income areas being able to make it to school without a parent there.

Yeah, I would say that among many, many, many other factors are one of the factors that I think you'll see more about next week when we look at our KPIs, at our kind of decision-making metrics will be applying to scenarios. Necessarily, there will be some shifts in boundaries that would have to happen if there are buildings that are closing or programs that are moving, but student safety is one of the pillars the board has set out for us and will be one of the principles we're looking at.

Yeah, I appreciate the question and thinking about student experience. This, you're surfacing a trade-off, and part of what will happen is when we look at school closure, it does mean the world will change the boundary, and that means that what that impact is on student travel, we're looking at. To your point, we're also looking at what are the major thoroughfares and safety and some of those pieces that that were that will take that into consideration. Part of what will happen as we go through is that it will be a description of: you know, here are there are a number of things in board policy that we need to consider, as well as the guiding principles that the board voted to shape this process. So we'll be reporting back what, as we're working through this process, where are those trade-offs? What does that look like? And what you're describing is sort of as the number of school sites, if they are smaller, may lead to longer transition times. That is true. And so we have to look at the specifics by where we are in the city and what does that mean. But I think that this is inherently, there will be some trade-offs that surface.

Same with feeder patterns and that type of thing. Like, we'll start to see our cohorts of students able to move through the system more together more frequently. And so, again, the scenarios as we bring them forward, we'll highlight what some of those trade-offs are. And that'll be part of the discussion of how do we weigh those.

Okay, and then my last question. I'm sorry, I'm asking a lot of hard questions. This one's going to be hard too. I'm warning you. So, how will right-sizing affect enrollment if we're changing neighborhood schools, like, are there projected ideas on how enrollment might change and if more or less kids will leave P or leave PPS because of their not being a school as close?

There are, we do use projections, that is true, and we do have to make some assumptions about how students will move through the system. What we saw in some of the decisions that came from the Southeast enrollment balancing is that when we move, for example, a program that we did not see students necessarily leave the district, but they may not have moved with the program. So there will be some things that we're going to have to make some decisions about, and as we go through, we have to. And so, we will be using projections, and some of those we will track over time to see how you know, see how we're doing relative to the projections. But I think the notion of inherently if there's a change, did people necessarily leave the district? That has not been what we've seen to this point.
Okay. Um, thank you. Thank you.
Thank you. Do you want a minute?

Let's do it. Hi, I didn't get to introduce myself. I'm Christy Split. I'm the board director for Zone 1, which is Southwest Portland. And grateful to be here. I had a previous commitment to be in Salem today with coworkers that were presenting to a committee there, and sorry that I was late as a result. So I always joke whenever you get me in the car, you're actually getting the best of me because I usually am like laser-focused. It's like the best focus you can get out of me is if I'm like doing something else at the same time as I'm listening to something. So it was really great to hear that presentation, especially because when I saw the slide that listed out some of the things we were aiming for, it was hard for me to understand why, because so many of the schools I visited have those things going on, where we do have music once a week and art once a week and things like that, because we aren't those lowest enrolled schools that I've been able to visit in my limited tenure and limited capacity to go visit schools during the day. I'd love to come. I probably do need to go and see some of the other schools outside of where I've been able to go so far. I've made a commitment to visit all the Zone 1 schools, and I think I pretty much got there,

but I maybe need to get out of my zone to see where there are these experiences that Director Sullivan mentioned where we're not reaching those criteria already. So that was, I guess, kind of my first question: I think it would be good to know because, like, I was trying to articulate this last time, but like, if people feel good about their experience and you're telling them, we know you feel good, but you're like, wrong. Like, in fact, you should expect better, and here's why. That's like a little hard to handle. And, like, um, and you know, when we have so many people that love their school so much and feel so good about where their kids are going to school, and I know they's exceptions to that. I just haven't heard from them enough. And so, but I guess maybe I've heard from a couple. But my question is really: like, have you done that analysis of like where there are those schools that already are hitting those targets. And I understand the traveling staff. That is a huge concern of mine. So that's probably the underlying, like, why I'm supportive of right-sizing in general,

it is like, I realized that's inconvenient and it leads to educators leaving the system to go to places where they can just be in one place all day. I mean, we're seeing it in one of my kids' schools where the art teacher that got assigned to our school elected not to come last minute. So now we don't have an R teacher at the beginning of the year. So I know those complexities that happen happen all over the place. So I'm curious: like, are you, do you have a list where you're like, these 30 schools have all the things we're going for, and these ones don't. So that way you kind of know where you've got the challenges, where people are gonna be like, you're telling me you're gonna make their experience better, but it's actually gonna be the same. Have you done any analysis of that? Does that make sense?

Yeah, so I guess I'm going to back up a little bit to where you started, and then we can talk more about analysis. We've been doing a lot of analysis. I think Philippe said earlier, and is absolutely right: like our teachers and principals and educators do a fabulous job taking whatever we give them and making it excellent for kids and families, right? And when we think in particular about the art and music example, we do right now make sure that every elementary student gets an arts every week, PE twice a week, library wide. Like there are certain core program requirements that we make it true for every elementary student right now. And we have stretched people incredibly thin to make that happen. And the cost of that is not only what you brought up, which is staff retention and just what it feels like to be a teacher working across three different schools in one week, having to know hundreds and hundreds more kids than you would if you were in one building, is the impact on the program. So there's a big difference. I was an elementary principal for a long time, there's a big difference between having an art teacher in your building one or two days a week who can make sure everybody gets a weekly art class, to having an arts teacher more or most of the week who can have a full arts program, who can do arts nights,

who can collaborate with the classroom teachers to have projects that extend what they're reading into art projects, right? Like, it's a different kind of a program that we're able to offer when we're at that very stretched model. And we have lots of schools in that situation right now, as Philippe shared. yeah.
I mean, as recently as three years ago, we had a full-time art teacher.

So I get it. And that's the current state. The other piece that we're hoping to get across, and we don't want to be alarmist, but this is our job, which is to say: looking ahead, the future isn't status quo. The future isn't we do this a few more years. And again, it's hard to predict the future, it's hard to predict funding and staffing and all that, but we know we're projected to have a budget deficit of 65 million this year. And that stretching is what we believe to be at capacity. And that is why there's such a need to reconsider resource reallocation and more intentional distribution of the resources that we have so that we don't have such imbalances of students' experiences across the school district, which are hard to, if we just step back, it's hard to justify that. So that's why this well-resourced school vision and framework is so important to us to say that let's go back to what we all believe to be true and what we want to be true for all our students and think about what are the adjustments that we need to make in order to make that happen.
So, is maybe what you're saying there are no schools that are currently well-resourced?
At the elementary level?
Sure. Yeah, because I think in terms of these metrics, there's a very small handful.
Yeah. You don't have to name the schools. I'm just curious. Are there some? I think a very small handful at this point.

Yeah, and I think, you know, part of what, you know, as we go through and describe some of this is the balance of feasible and aspirational is going to be present throughout, right? And I would say that when we look at well-resourced schools and we do descriptors,

regardless of the level, we often hold an elementary mindset. That's the place that our minds go instantly. And what we see, part of what happened when we did some of the middle school redesign process, was to say, how do we getting comparable programming to every middle grade student given the variety of spaces that we're seeing. And so I think that there are, we can get closer to what that includes and what those pieces are. And I think that, like, when we did this with some of the academic comparisons when we were looking at high schools, as part of the sunsetting of Jefferson dual assignment, you get a sense of: is there a baseline that we're holding for everyone? And then, is there what is can we get closer to that? So, some people, some schools may have some things, but not others, and so can we get closer to more schools making progress towards this is really what we're gonna see. And I would say that what we know is that this is coming to middle schools, and so we may not have felt it in the same way just yet. Just yet, if that makes sense.

I, for my day job, spend a lot of time talking about data centers and energy demand projections for the state, and we always show a slide that says all models are wrong, some are useful. Feel free to borrow it. It's a quote, not for me. I can attribute it later. I don't remember the person right now, but we have it on all of our slides whenever we talk to legislators about increasing demand. And I guess I hope that you consider that too, because we are talking about models and forecasts, and they can change. And so I always I've always had like some level of skepticism about the like post-COVID experience in Portland and like is that gonna be the future of our city or, not?
